assessment_summary:
I attempted to prove the statement using a standard exchange argument.
Step 1: Let G be the schedule produced by the shortest-duration greedy algorithm, and O be an optimal schedule.
Step 2: Let g_1 be the first interval selected by the greedy algorithm. By definition, g_1 has the minimum duration among all available intervals.
Step 3: Suppose g_1 is not in O. We can swap g_1 with some interval in O (or add it while removing at most one interval) to create a new valid schedule O' of at least the same size.
Flawed Step: Step 3 is definitively unjustified. Selecting g_1 might force us to remove multiple disjoint intervals from O because g_1 can overlap with more than one interval in the optimal schedule. In such cases, swapping g_1 into O reduces the total number of non-overlapping intervals, breaking the optimality.
counterexample:
Consider the set of three intervals: A = [0, 10), B = [9, 11), C = [10, 22).
Their durations are 10, 2, and 12 respectively. All durations are distinct, so there are no tie-breaking ambiguities.
The optimal schedule selects A and C, which are pairwise non-overlapping (they meet exactly at 10 but do not intersect since intervals are half-open). The optimal size is 2.
The shortest-duration greedy algorithm selects B first, since it has the shortest duration (2).
Interval B = [9, 11) conflicts with A = [0, 10) (intersection is [9, 10)) and also conflicts with C = [10, 22) (intersection is [10, 11)). 
Thus, A and C are both discarded. The greedy algorithm terminates with a schedule size of 1.
Since 1 < 2, the greedy algorithm strictly fails to yield a maximum-size schedule.
